revisions.title: From crowd to a local epistemic asymmetry
revisions.body: The exchange pivots on a narrowing qualification. Gorgias’s claim that rhetoric persuades more than medicine is first limited to a crowd; Socrates recasts that crowd as people who do not know, producing the local result that the non-knower can persuade non-knowers more effectively than the knower. Gorgias grants that consequence here, but the record does not establish that he accepts it as a universal rule. Socrates nevertheless extends the pattern to rhetoric generally: persuasion can make ignorance appear as knowledge. One way to hear the pressure point is as a gap between a case-specific concession and a general theory.

Socrates then generalizes: rhetoric need not know the matters themselves; it needs a device that makes ignorance look like knowledge. The question becomes whether persuasion can substitute for expertise."
